entries.ed6c6342078ba9db5f818045a550e8e4a41f0e87: <div sID="gen20152" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Amos.5" sID="Amos.5"/> <div eID="gen20152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20153" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20154" type="x-p"/> The scope of this chapter is to prosecute the exhortation given to Israel in the close of the foregoing chapter to prepare to meet their God; the prophet here tells them, I. What preparation they must make; they must "seek the Lord," and not seek any more to idols (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.4-Amos.5.8">ver. 4-8</reference>); they must seek good, and love it, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14-Amos.5.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. II. Why they must make this preparation to meet their God, 1. Because of the present deplorable condition they were in, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.1-Amos.5.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. Because it was by sin that they were brought into such a condition, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">ver. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10-Amos.5.12">10-12</reference>. 3. Because it would be their happiness to seek God, and he was ready to be found of them, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8-Amos.5.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">14</reference>. 4. Because he would proceed, in his wrath, to their utter ruin, if they did not seek him, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5-Amos.5.6 Amos.5.13 Amos.5.16 Amos.5.17">ver. 5, 6, 13, 16, 17</reference>. 5. Because all their confidences would fail them if they did not seek unto God, and make him their friend. (1.) Their profane contempt of God's judgments, and setting them at defiance, would not secure them, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18-Amos.5.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. (2.) Their external services in religion, and the shows of devotion, would not avail to turn away the wrath of God, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21-Amos.5.24">ver. 21-24</reference>. (3.) Their having been long in possession of church-privileges, and in a course of holy duties, would not be their protection, while all along they had kept up their idolatrous customs, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.25-Amos.5.27">ver. 25-27</reference>. They have therefore no way left them to save themselves, but by repentance and reformation.
entries.11692d1c14a175530e0a4a48d30ed900cd64db30: <div eID="gen20154" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20153" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Invitations and Warnings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20155" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear ye this word which I take up against you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a lamentation, O house of Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> The virgin of Israel is fallen; she shall no more rise: she is forsaken upon her land; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to raise her up. <hi type="super">3</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; The city that went out <hi type="italic">by</hi> a thousand shall leave a hundred, and that which went forth <hi type="italic">by</hi> a hundred shall leave ten, to the house of Israel. <div eID="gen20155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20156" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins, as those two next foregoing began, with, <hi type="italic">Hear this word.</hi> Where God has a mouth to speak we must have an ear to hear; it is our duty, it is our interest, yet so stupid are most men that they need to be again and again called upon to <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord,</hi> to give audience, to give attention. <hi type="italic">Hear this word.</hi> this convincing awakening word must be heard and heeded, as well as words of comfort and peace; the word that is taken up against us, as well as that which makes for us; for, whether we hear or forbear, the word of God shall take effect, and not a tittle of it shall fall to the ground. It is the <hi type="italic">word which I take up</hi>—not the prophet only, but the God that sent him. It is <hi type="italic">the word that the Lord has spoken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>. The word to be heard is <hi type="italic">a lamentation,</hi> a lamentable account of the present calamitous state of the kingdom of Israel, and a lamentable prediction of its utter destruction. Their condition is sad: <hi type="italic">The virgin of Israel has fallen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.2">v. 2</reference>), has come down from what she was; that state, though not pure and chaste as a virgin, yet was beautiful and gay, and had its charms; she looked high herself, and was courted by many as a virgin; but <hi type="italic">she has fallen</hi> into contempt and poverty, and is universally slighted. Nay, and their condition is helpless: <hi type="italic">She shall no more rise,</hi> shall never recover her former dignity again. God had lately begun to <hi type="italic">cut Israel short</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2 Kings x. 32</reference>), and, because they repented not, it was not long before he <hi type="italic">cut Israel down.</hi> 1. Their princes, that should have helped them up, were disabled: <hi type="italic">She is forsaken upon her land.</hi> Not only those she was in alliance with abroad failed her, but her friends at home deserted her; she would not have been carried captive into a strange land if she had not first been <hi type="italic">forsaken upon her own land</hi> and <hi type="italic">thrown to the ground</hi> there, and all her true interests abandoned by those that should have had them at heart. <hi type="italic">There is none to raise her up,</hi> none that can do it, not that cares to lend her a hand. 2. Their people, that should have helped them up, were diminished, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.3">v. 3</reference>. "The city that had a militia, 1000 strong, and, in the beginning of the war, had furnished out 1000 effective men, able-bodied and well-armed, when they come to review their troops after the battle, shall find but 100 <hi type="italic">left;</hi> and, in proportion, the city that sent out 100 shall have but <hi type="italic">ten</hi> come back, so great a slaughter shall be made, and so few left to the house of Israel for the public service and safety." Scarcely one in ten shall escape of the hands that should relieve this abject, this dejected, nation. Note, The lessening of the numbers of God's spiritual Israel, by death or desertion, is just a matter for lamentation; for <hi type="italic">by whom shall Jacob arise,</hi> by whom shall the decays of piety be repaired, when he is thus <hi type="italic">made small?</hi>
entries.13fa97bfed125d4d4f44735cc15080c76ccb18dd: <div eID="gen20156" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Message to Israel; The Aggravated Sins of Israel; Warnings and Exhortations; Exhortations and Encouragements. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  790.)</title> <div sID="gen20157" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live: <hi type="super">5</hi> But seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and pass not to Beer-sheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nought. <hi type="super">6</hi> Seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and devour <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there be</hi> none to quench <hi type="italic">it</hi> in Bethel. <hi type="super">7</hi> Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth, <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">Seek him</hi> that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning, and maketh the day dark with night: that calleth for the waters of the sea, and poureth them out upon the face of the earth: The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name: <hi type="super">9</hi> That strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong, so that the spoiled shall come against the fortress. <hi type="super">10</hi> They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. <hi type="super">11</hi> Forasmuch therefore as your treading <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the poor, and ye take from him burdens of wheat: ye have built houses of hewn stone, but ye shall not dwell in them; ye have planted pleasant vineyards, but ye shall not drink wine of them. <hi type="super">12</hi> For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate <hi type="italic">from their right.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an evil time. <hi type="super">14</hi> Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live: and so the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of hosts, shall be with you, as ye have spoken. <hi type="super">15</hi> Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate: it may be that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of hosts will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph. <div eID="gen20157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20158" type="x-p"/> This is a message from God to the house of Israel, in which, <div eID="gen20158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20159" type="x-p"/> I. They are told of their faults, that they might see what occasion there was for them to repent and reform, and that, when they were called to return, they might not need to ask, <hi type="italic">Wherein shall we return?</hi> <div eID="gen20159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20160" type="x-p"/> 1. God tells them, in general (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.12">v. 12</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I know your manifold transgressions, and your mighty sins;</hi> and you shall be made to know them too." In our penitent reflections upon our sins we must consider, as God does in his judicial remarks upon them, and will do in the great day, (1.) That they are very numerous; they are our <hi type="italic">manifold transgressions,</hi> sins of various kinds and often repeated. Oh what a multitude of vain and vile thoughts lodge within us! What a multitude of idle, foolish, wicked words have been spoken by us! In what a multitude of instances have we gratified and indulged our corrupt appetites and passions! And how many our own omissions of duty and in duty! Who can understand his errors? Who can tell how often he offends? God knows how many, just how many, our transgressions are; none of them pass him unobserved; we know that they are to us innumerable; <hi type="italic">more than the hairs of our head;</hi> and we have reason to see what danger we have brought ourselves into, and what abundance of work we have made for repentance, by our <hi type="italic">manifold transgressions,</hi> by the numberless number of our sins of daily incursion. (2.) That some of them are very heinous; they are <hi type="italic">our mighty</hi> sins; sins that are more exceedingly sinful in their own nature and by being committed presumptuously and with a high hand, sins against the light of nature, flagrant crimes, that are mighty to overpower your convictions and to pull down judgments upon you. <div eID="gen20160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20161" type="x-p"/> 2. He specifies some of these mighty sins. (1.) They corrupted the worship of God, and turned to idols; this is implied <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">v. 5</reference>. They had <hi type="italic">sought to Bethel,</hi> where one of the golden calves was; they had frequented Gilgal, a place which they chose to set up idols in, because it had been made famous in the days of Joshua by God's wonderful appearances to and for his people. Beer-sheba likewise, a place that had been famous in the days of the patriarchs, was now another rendezvous of idols; as we find also, <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">ch. viii. 14</reference>. And thither <hi type="italic">they passed,</hi> though it lay at a distance, in the land of Judah. Now, having thus shamefully gone a whoring from God, no doubt they should have felt themselves concerned to return to him. (2.) They perverted justice among themselves (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You turn judgment to wormwood,</hi> that is, you make your administrations of justice bitter and nauseous, and highly displeasing both to God and man." That fruit has become a <hi type="italic">weed,</hi> a weed in the garden; as nothing is more venerable, nothing more valuable, than justice duly administered, so nothing is more hurtful, nothing more abominable, than designedly doing wrong under colour and pretence of doing right. <hi type="italic">Corruptio optimi est pessima</hi>—<hi type="italic">The best, when corrupted, becomes the worst. "You leave off righteousness in the earth,</hi> as if those that do wrong were accountable to the God of heaven only, and not to the princes and <hi type="italic">judges of the earth.</hi>" Thus it was as before the flood, when the <hi type="italic">earth was filled with violence.</hi> (3.) They were very oppressive to the poor, and made them poorer; they trod upon the poor (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">v. 11</reference>), trampled upon them, hectored over them, made them their footstool, and were most imperious and barbarous to those that were most obsequious and submissive; they care not what shame and slavery they put those to who were poor and such as they could get nothing by. The judges aimed at nothing but to enrich themselves; and therefore they <hi type="italic">took from</hi> the poor <hi type="italic">burdens of wheat,</hi> took it by extortion, either by way of bribe or by usury. The poor had no other way to save themselves from being trodden upon, and trodden to dirt, by them, than by presenting to them horse-loads of that corn which they and their families should have had to subsist upon, and they forced them to do it. They took from the poor <hi type="italic">debts of wheat,</hi> so some read it. It was legally due either for rent or for corn lent, but they exacted it with rigour from those who were disabled by the providence of God to pay it, as <reference osisRef="Neh.5.2">Neh. v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.5">5</reference>. In demanding and recovering even a just debt we must take heed lest we act either unjustly or uncharitably. This sin of oppression by are again charged with (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They afflict the just,</hi> by turning the edge of the law and of the sword of justice against those that are the innocent and <hi type="italic">quiet in the land;</hi> they hated men because they were more righteous than themselves, and he that <hi type="italic">departed from evil</hi> thereby <hi type="italic">made himself a prey</hi> to them. They take a bribe from the rich to patronize and protect them in oppressing the poor, so that he who has money in his hand is sure to have the judgment on his side, be his cause ever so bad. Thus they <hi type="italic">turn aside the poor in the gate,</hi> in the courts of justice, <hi type="italic">from their right.</hi> If the poor sue for their right, who cannot bribe them, or are so honest that they will not, though they have it ever so clear in view and ever so <hi type="italic">near,</hi> yet they are turned away from it by their unrighteous sentence and cannot come at it. And <hi type="italic">therefore the prudent will keep silence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">v. 13</reference>. Men will reckon it their prudence, when they are wronged and injured, to be silent, and make no complaints to the magistrates, for it will be to no purpose; they shall not have justice done them. (4.) They were malicious persecutors of God's faithful ministers and people, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10">v. 10</reference>. Their hearts were so fully set in them to do evil that they could not bear to be reproved, [1.] By the ministry of the word, by the reading and expounding of the law, and the messages which prophets delivered to them in the name of the Lord. <hi type="italic">They hate him that rebukes in the gate,</hi> in the gate of the Lord's house, or in their courts of justice, or in the places of concourse, where Wisdom is lifting up her voice, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>. Reprovers in the gate are reprovers by office; these they hated, counting them their <hi type="italic">enemies because they told them the truth,</hi> as Ahab hated Micaiah. They not only despised them, but had an enmity to them, and sought to do them mischief. Those that hate reproof love ruin. [2.] By the conversation of their honest neighbours. Though things were generally very bad, yet there were some among them that <hi type="italic">spoke uprightly</hi> that made conscience of what they said, and, as it was their praise, so it was the shame of those that spoke deceitfully, and condemned them, as Noah's faith condemned the unbelief of the old world, and for that reason <hi type="italic">they abhorred them;</hi> they were such inveterate enemies to the thing called honesty that they could not endure the sight of an honest man. All that have any sense of the common interest of mankind will love and value such as speak uprightly, for veracity is the bond of human society; to what a pitch of folly and madness then have those arrived who, having banished all notions of justice out of their own hearts, would have them banished out of the world too, and so put mankind into a state of war, for they <hi type="italic">abhor him that speaks uprightly!</hi> And for this reason <hi type="italic">the prudent shall keep silence in that time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">v. 13</reference>. Prophets cannot, dare not, keep silence; the impulse they are under will not allow them to act on prudential considerations; they must <hi type="italic">cry aloud, and not spare.</hi> But as for other wise and good men they shall keep silence, and shall reckon it is their prudence to do so, because it is an evil time. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They shall think it dangerous to complain, and therefore shall keep silence; this was one way in which they afflicted the just, that by false suggestions and strained innuendos they made men <hi type="italic">offenders for a word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.21">Isa. xix. 21</reference>); and therefore the <hi type="italic">prudent,</hi> who were <hi type="italic">wise as serpents,</hi> because they knew not how what they said might be misinterpreted and misrepresented, were so cautious as to say nothing, lest they should run themselves into a premunire, because it was an evil time. Note, Through the iniquity of the times, as good men are hidden, so good men are silent, and it is their wisdom to be so; <hi type="italic">little said soon amended.</hi> But it is their comfort that they may speak freely to God when they know not to whom else they can speak freely. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They shall think if fruitless to reprove. They see what wickedness is committed, and their spirits are stirred up, as Paul's at Athens; but they shall think it prudent not to bear an open testimony against it, because it is to no purpose. They are <hi type="italic">joined to their idols; let them alone. Let no man strive or rebuke another;</hi> for it is but <hi type="italic">casting pearls before swine.</hi> The cautious men will say to a bold reprover, as Erasmus to Luther, "<hi type="italic">Abi in cellam, et dic, Miserere mei, Domine</hi>—<hi type="italic">Away to thy cell, and cry, Have mercy on me, O Lord!</hi>" Let grave lessons and counsels be kept for better men and better times. And there is <hi type="italic">a time to keep silence</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">a time to speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.7">Eccl. iii. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Evil times</hi> will not bear plain dealing, that is <hi type="italic">evil men</hi> will not; and the men the prophet here speaks of had reason to think themselves evil men indeed, when wise and good men thought it in vain to speak to them and were afraid of having any thing to do with them. <div eID="gen20161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20162" type="x-p"/> II. They are told of their danger and what judgments they lay exposed to for their sins. 1. The places of their idolatry are in danger of being ruined in the first place, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Gilgal,</hi> the head-quarters of idolatry, <hi type="italic">shall go into captivity,</hi> not only its inhabitants, but its images, <hi type="italic">and Bethel,</hi> with its golden calf <hi type="italic">shall come to nought.</hi> The victorious enemy shall make nothing of it, so easily shall it be spoiled, and shall bring it to nothing, so effectually shall it be spoiled. Idols were always vanity, and <hi type="italic">things of nought,</hi> and so they shall prove when God appears to abolish them. 2. The body of the kingdom is in danger of being ruined with them, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">v. 6</reference>. There is danger lest, if you seek him not in time, he <hi type="italic">break out like a fire in the house of Joseph and devour it;</hi> for our God is a righteous Judge, is a <hi type="italic">consuming fire,</hi> and the men of Israel, as criminals, are stubble before him; woe to those that make themselves fuel to the fire of God's wrath. It follows, <hi type="italic">And there shall be none to quench it in Bethel.</hi> There their idols were, and their idolatrous priests; thither they brought their sacrifices, and there they offered up their prayers. But God tells them that when the fire of his judgments should kindle upon them all the gods they served at Bethel should not be able to quench it, should not turn away the judgment, nor be any relief to them under it. Thus those that make an idol of the world will find it insufficient to protect them when God comes to reckon with them for their spiritual idolatry. 3. What they have got by oppression and extortion shall be taken from them (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You have built houses of hewn stone,</hi> which you thought would be lasting; <hi type="italic">but you shall not dwell in them,</hi> for your enemies shall burn them down, or possess them for themselves, or take you into captivity. <hi type="italic">You have planted pleasant vineyards,</hi> have contrived how to make them every way agreeable, and have promised yourselves many a pleasant walk in them; but you shall be forced to walk off, and shall never <hi type="italic">drink wine of them.</hi>" The law had tenderly provided that if a man had <hi type="italic">built a house,</hi> or <hi type="italic">planted a vineyard,</hi> he should be at his liberty to return from the wars, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.5-Deut.20.6">Deut. xx. 5, 6</reference>. But now the necessity would be so urgent that it would not be allowed; all must go to the battle, and many of those who had lately been building and planting should fall in battle, and never enjoy what they had been labouring for. What is not honestly got is not likely to be long enjoyed. <div eID="gen20162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20163" type="x-p"/> III. They are told their duty, and have great encouragement to set about it in good earnest, and good reason. The duties here prescribed to them are godliness and honesty, seriousness in their applications to God and justice in their dealings with men; and each of these is here pressed upon them with proper arguments to enforce the exhortation. <div eID="gen20163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20164" type="x-p"/> 1. They are here exhorted to be sincere and devout in their addresses to God, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">v. 4</reference>. God says to the <hi type="italic">house of Israel, Seek you me,</hi> and with good reason, for <hi type="italic">should not a people seek unto their God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>. Whither else should they go but to their protector? Israel was a <hi type="italic">prince with God;</hi> let his descendants <hi type="italic">seek the Lord,</hi> as he did, and they shall be so too. Now, in order to their doing this, they must abandon their idolatries. God is not sought truly if he be not sought exclusively, for he will endure no rivals: "<hi type="italic">Seek you the Lord, and seek not Bethel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">v. 5</reference>), consult not your idol-oracles, nor ask at the mouth of the priests of Bethel; seek not to the golden calf there for protection, nor bring your prayers and sacrifices any longer thither, or to Gilgal, for you <hi type="italic">forsake your own mercies</hi> if you observe those <hi type="italic">lying vanities.</hi> But <hi type="italic">seek the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">8</reference>); enquire after him; enquire of him; seek to know his mind as your rule, to secure his favour as your felicity." To press this exhortation we are told to consider, (1.) What we shall get by seeking God; it will be <hi type="italic">our life;</hi> we shall find him, and shall be happy in him. So he tells them himself (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Seek you me, and you shall live.</hi> Those that seek perishing gods shall perish with them (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">v. 5</reference>), but those that seek the living God shall live with him: "You shall be delivered from the killing judgments which you are threatened with; your nation shall live, shall recover from its present languishings; your souls shall live; you shall be sanctified and comforted, and made for ever blessed. <hi type="italic">You shall live.</hi>" (2.) What a God he is whom we are to <hi type="italic">seek,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8-Amos.5.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. [1.] He is a God of almighty power himself. The idols were impotent things, could do neither good nor evil, and therefore it was folly either to fear or trust them; but the God of Israel does every thing, and can do any thing, and therefore we ought to seek him; he challenges our homage who has all power in his hand, and it is our interest to have him on our side. Divers proofs and instances are here given of God's power, as Creator, in the kingdom of nature, as both founding and governing that kingdom. Compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">ch. iv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The stars are the work of his hands; those stars which the heathens worshipped (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">v. 26</reference>), the <hi type="italic">stars of your god,</hi> those stars are God's creatures and servants. He <hi type="italic">makes the seven stars and Orion,</hi> two very remarkable constellations, which Amos, a herdsman, while he kept his cattle by night, had particularly observed the motions of. He made them at the first, he still makes them to be what they are to this earth and either <hi type="italic">binds</hi> or <hi type="italic">looses</hi> the <hi type="italic">sweet influences of Peliades</hi> and <hi type="italic">Orion,</hi> the two constellations here mentioned. See <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job xxxviii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">ix. 9</reference>, to which passages Amos seems here to refer, putting them in mind of those ancient discoveries of the glory of God before he was called the <hi type="italic">God of Israel. Secondly,</hi> The constant succession of day and night is under his direction, and is kept up by his power and providence. It is he that <hi type="italic">turns</hi> the night (which is dark as <hi type="italic">the shadow of death</hi>) <hi type="italic">into the morning</hi> by the rising of the sun, and by the setting of the sun <hi type="italic">makes the day dark with night;</hi> and the same power can, for humble penitents, easily turn affliction and sorrow into prosperity and joy, but can as easily turn the prosperity of presumptuous sinners into darkness, into utter darkness. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The rain rises and falls as he appoints. He <hi type="italic">calls for the waters of the sea;</hi> out of them vapours are drawn up by the heat of the sun, which gather into clouds, and are <hi type="italic">poured out upon the face of the earth,</hi> to water it and make it fruitful. This was the mercy that had been <hi type="italic">withholden from them</hi> of late (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>); and therefore to whom should they apply but to him who had power to give it? For all the <hi type="italic">vanities of the heathen</hi> could not <hi type="italic">give rain,</hi> nor could the <hi type="italic">heavens</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">give showers</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jer. xiv. 22</reference>. It is God that has <hi type="italic">made these things; Jehovah is his name,</hi> the name by which the God of nature, the God of the whole earth, has made himself known to his people Israel and covenanted with them. [2.] As he is God of almighty power himself, so he <hi type="italic">gives strength and power unto his people</hi> that seek him, and <hi type="italic">renews strength</hi> to those that had lost it, if they <hi type="italic">wait upon him</hi> for it; for (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.9">v. 9</reference>) he <hi type="italic">strengthens the spoiled against the strong</hi> to such a degree that the spoiled come <hi type="italic">against the fortress</hi> and make bold and brave attacks upon those that had spoiled them. This is an encouragement to the people to <hi type="italic">seek the Lord,</hi> that, if they do so, they shall find him above to retrieve their affairs, when they are brought to the lowest ebb; though they are the spoiled, and their enemies are the strong, if they can but engage God for them, they shall soon recruit so as the next time to be not only the aggressors, but the conquerors; they <hi type="italic">come against the fortress,</hi> to make reprisals and become masters of it. <div eID="gen20164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20165" type="x-p"/> 2. They are here exhorted to be honest and just in their dealings with men, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14-Amos.5.15">v. 14, 15</reference>, where observe, (1.) The duty required: <hi type="italic">Seek good, and not evil. Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate;</hi> re-establish it there, whence it has been banished, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, Things are not so bad but that they may be amended if the right course be taken; we must not despair but that grievances may be redressed and abuses rectified; justice may yet triumph where injustice tyrannizes. In order to this, good must be loved and sought, evil must be hated and no longer sought. We must love good principles and adhere to them, love to do good and abound in doing it, love good people, and good converse, and good duties; and, whatever good we do, we must do it from a principle of love, do it of choice and with delight. Those who thus <hi type="italic">love good</hi> will <hi type="italic">seek it,</hi> will contrive to do all the good they can, enquire for opportunities of doing it, and endeavor to do it to the utmost of their power. They will also <hi type="italic">hate evil,</hi> will abhor the thought of doing an unjust thing, and abstain from all appearance of it. In vain do we pretend to seek God in our devotions if we do not seek good in our whole conversations. (2.) The reasons annexed. [1.] This is the sure way to be happy ourselves and to have the continual presence of God with us: "<hi type="italic">Seek good, and not evil, that you may live,</hi> may escape the punishment of the evil you have sought and loved (<hi type="italic">righteousness delivereth from death</hi>), that you may have the favour of God, which is your life, which is better than life itself, that you may have comfort in yourselves and may live to some good purpose. You shall live, for <hi type="italic">so the Lord God of hosts shall be with you</hi> and be your life." Note, Those that keep in the way of duty have the presence of God with them, as the <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> a God of almighty power. "He will be with you <hi type="italic">as you have spoken,</hi> that is, as you have <hi type="italic">gloried;</hi> you shall have that really which, while you went on in unrighteous ways, you only seemed to have and boasted of as if you had." Those that truly repent and reform enter into the enjoyment of that comfort which before they had only flattered themselves with the imagination of. Or, "As you have prayed when <hi type="italic">you sought the Lord.</hi> Live up to your prayers, and you shall have what you pray for." [2.] This is the likeliest way to make the nation happy: "If you seek and love that which is good, you may contribute to the saving of the land from ruin." <hi type="italic">It may be, the Lord God of hosts will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph;</hi> though there is but a remnant left, yet, if God be gracious to that remnant, it will rise to a great nation again; and if some among them turn from sin, especially if <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> be <hi type="italic">established in the gate,</hi> though we cannot be certain, yet there is a great probability that public affairs will take a new and happy turn, and every thing will mend if men mend their lives. Temporary promises are made with an <hi type="italic">It may be;</hi> and our prayers must be made accordingly.
entries.12b03af26a895d4220fe4577681de69715dff6b7: <div eID="gen20165" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings and Reproofs. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of hosts, the Lord, saith thus; Wailing <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in all streets; and they shall say in all the highways, Alas! alas! and they shall call the husbandman to mourning, and such as are skilful of lamentation to wailing. <hi type="super">17</hi> And in all vineyards <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> wailing: for I will pass through thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> Woe unto you that desire the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ! to what end <hi type="italic">is</hi> it for you? the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> darkness, and not light. <hi type="super">19</hi> As if a man did flee from a lion, and a bear met him; or went into the house, and leaned his hand on the wall, and a serpent bit him. <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">Shall</hi> not the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> darkness, and not light? even very dark, and no brightness in it? <div eID="gen20166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20167" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A very terrible threatening of destruction approaching, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16-Amos.5.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Since they would not take the right course to obtain the favour of God, God would take an effectual course to make them feel the weight of his displeasure. The threatening is introduced with more than ordinary solemnity, to strike an awe upon them; it is not the word of the prophet only (if so, it might be made light of) but it is the <hi type="italic">Lord Jehovah,</hi> who has an infinite eternal being; it is the <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> who has a boundless irresistible power, and it is <hi type="italic">Adonai—the Lord,</hi> who has an absolute incontestable sovereignty, and a universal dominion; it is he who says it, who can and will make his words good, and he has said, 1. That the land of Israel shall be put in mourning, true mourning, that all places shall be filled with lamentation for the calamities coming upon them. Look into the cities, and <hi type="italic">wailing shall be in all streets,</hi> in the great streets, in the by-streets. Look into the country, and <hi type="italic">they shall say in all the highways, Alas! alas!</hi> we are all undone! The lamentation shall be so great as not to be confined within doors, nor kept within the bounds of decency, but it shall be proclaimed in the streets and highways, and shall run wild. The husbandman shall be called from the plough by the calamities of his country to the natural expressions of mourning; and, because those who will come short of the merits of the cause, such as are skilful of lamentation shall be called to artificial mourning, to put accents upon the lamentations of the real mourners with their <hi type="italic">Ahone, ahone.</hi> Even in all vineyards, where there used to be nothing but mirth and pleasure, there shall be general wailing, when a foreign force invades the country, lays all waste, and there is no making any head against it, no weapons left but prayers and tears. 2. That the land of Israel shall be brought to ruin, and the advances of that ruin are the occasion of all this wailing: <hi type="italic">I will pass through thee,</hi> as the destroying angel passed through the land of Egypt to destroy the first-born, but then passed over the houses of the Israelites. God's judgments had often passed by them, but now they shall pass through them, shall run them through. <div eID="gen20167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20168" type="x-p"/> II. A just and severe reproof to those who made light of these threatenings, and impudently bade defiance to the justice of God and his judgments, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">v. 18</reference>. Woe unto you that <hi type="italic">desire the day of the Lord,</hi> that really wish for times of war and confusion, as some do who have restless spirits, and long for changes, or who choose to <hi type="italic">fish in troubled waters,</hi> hoping to raise their families, as some had done, upon the ruins of their country; but the prophet tells them that this should be so great a desolation that nobody could get by it. Or it is spoken to those who, in their wailings and lamentations for the calamities they were in, wished they might die, and be delivered out of their misery, as Job did, with passion. The prophet shows them the folly of this. Do they know what death is to those who are unprepared for it, and how much more terrible it will be than any thing that can befal them in this life? Or, rather, it is spoken to those who speak jestingly of that day of the Lord which the prophet spoke so seriously of; they desired it, that is, they challenged it; they said, Let him do his worst; <hi type="italic">let him make speed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hasten his work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa. v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 4</reference>. It intimates, 1. That they do not believe it. They say that they wish it would come because they do not believe it will ever come; nor will they believe it unless they see it. 2. That they do not fear it; though they may have some belief of it, yet they had so little consideration of it, and their mind is so intent upon other things, that they are under no apprehension at all of peril from it; instead of having the conscience to dread it, they have the curiosity to desire it. In answer to this, (1.) He shows the folly of those who impudently wished for any of God's judgments, and made a jest of any of the terrors of the Lord: "<hi type="italic">To what end is it for you</hi> that the day of the Lord should come? You will find it both certain and sad; not a thing to be bantered, for it is neither a thing to be questioned whether it will come or no nor a thing to be turned off with a slight when it does come. <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord is darkness, and not light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Shall it not be so?</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.20">v. 20</reference>. Do not your own consciences tell you that it will be so, that it will be <hi type="italic">very dark,</hi> and <hi type="italic">no brightness in it?</hi>" Note, The <hi type="italic">day of the Lord</hi> will be a dark, dismal, gloomy day to all impenitent sinners; the <hi type="italic">day of judgment</hi> will be so; and sometimes the day of their present trouble. And, when God makes a day dark, all the world cannot make it light. (2.) He shows the folly of those who impatiently wished for a change of God's judgment, in hopes that the next would be better and more tolerable. They desire <hi type="italic">the day of the Lord,</hi> in hopes to better themselves (though their hearts and lives be not amended), or, at least, to know the worst. But the prophet tells them that they know not what they ask, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">v. 19</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">as if a man did flee from a lion and a bear met him,</hi> a beast of prey more cruel and ravenous than a lion, or as if a man, to escape all dangers abroad, <hi type="italic">went into the house for security,</hi> and <hi type="italic">leaned his hand on the wall</hi> to rest himself, and there a <hi type="italic">serpent bit him.</hi> Note, Those who are not reformed by the judgments of God will be pursued by them; and, if they escape one, another stands ready to seize them; <hi type="italic">fear and the pit and snare</hi> surround them, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.17-Isa.24.18">Isa. xxiv. 17, 18</reference>. It is madness therefore to <hi type="italic">defy the day of the Lord.</hi>
entries.c77b868ef10a12718f76ddb74e09ed7b5c014cfc: <div eID="gen20168" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Hypocritical Services Rejected; Threatenings against Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20169" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies. <hi type="super">22</hi> Though ye offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept <hi type="italic">them:</hi> neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat beasts. <hi type="super">23</hi> Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. <hi type="super">24</hi> But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream. <hi type="super">25</hi> Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel? <hi type="super">26</hi> But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves. <hi type="super">27</hi> Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , whose name <hi type="italic">is</hi> The God of hosts. <div eID="gen20169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20170" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to show how little God valued their shows of devotion, nay, how much he detested them, while they went on in their sins. Observe, <div eID="gen20170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20171" type="x-p"/> I. How unpleasing, nay, how displeasing, their hypocritical services were to God. They had their <hi type="italic">feast-days</hi> at Bethel, in imitation of those at Jerusalem, in which they pretended to rejoice before God. They had their <hi type="italic">solemn assemblies</hi> for religious worship, in which they put on the gravity of those who <hi type="italic">come before God as his people come, and sit before him as his people sit.</hi> They offered to God <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings,</hi> to the honour of God, together with the <hi type="italic">meat-offerings</hi> which by the law were to be offered with them; they offered the <hi type="italic">peace-offerings,</hi> to implore the favour of God, and they offered them of the <hi type="italic">fat beasts</hi> that they had, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21-Amos.5.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. In imitation likewise of the temple-music, they had the <hi type="italic">noise of their songs</hi> and the <hi type="italic">melody of their viols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">v. 23</reference>), vocal and instrumental music, with which they praised God. With these services they hoped to make God amends for the sins they had committed, and to obtain leave to go on in sin; and therefore they were so far from being acceptable to God that they were abominable. He <hi type="italic">hated,</hi> he <hi type="italic">despised,</hi> their <hi type="italic">feast-days,</hi> not only despised them as no valuable services done to him, but hated them as an affront and provocation to him, as we hate to see men dissemble with us, pretend a respect for us when really they have none. Nothing more hateful, more despicable, than hypocrisy. <hi type="italic">He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, it shall be counted a curse,</hi> when it appears that his heart is not with him. God will not <hi type="italic">smell</hi> in <hi type="italic">their solemn assemblies,</hi> for there is nothing in them that is grateful to him, but a great deal that is offensive. Their sacrifices are not to him <hi type="italic">of a sweet smelling savour,</hi> as Noah's was, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen. viii. 21</reference>. He will not accept them; he will not regard them, will not take any notice of them; he will not hear the melody of their viols; for, when sin is a jar in the harmony, it grates in his ears: "<hi type="italic">Take it away,</hi>" says God, "I cannot bear it." Now this intimates, 1. That sacrifice itself is of small account with God in comparison with moral duties; to love God and our neighbour is <hi type="italic">better than all burnt offering and sacrifice.</hi> 2. That the sacrifice of the wicked is really an abomination to him, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>. Dissembled piety is double iniquity, and so it will be found when, if any place in hell be hotter than another, that will be the hypocrite's portion. <div eID="gen20171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20172" type="x-p"/> II. What it was that he required in order to the acceptableness of their sacrifices and without which no sacrifice would be acceptable (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let judgment run down as waters,</hi> among you, <hi type="italic">and righteousness as a mighty stream,</hi> that is 1. "Let there be a general reformation of manners among you; let religion (God's <hi type="italic">judgment</hi>) and <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> have their due influence upon you; let your land be watered with it, and let it bear down all the opposition of vice and profaneness; let it run wide as overflowing waters, and yet run strong as mighty stream." (2.) "In particular, let justice be duly administered by magistrates and rulers; let not the current of it be stopped by partiality and bribery, but let it come freely as waters do, in the natural course; let it be pure as running waters, not muddied with corruption or whatever may pervert justice; let it run <hi type="italic">like a mighty stream,</hi> and not suffer itself to be obstructed, or its course retarded, by the fear of man; let all have free access to it as a common stream, and have benefit by it as <hi type="italic">trees planted by the rivers of waters.</hi>" The great thing laid to Israel's charge was <hi type="italic">turning judgment into wormwood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">v. 7</reference>); in that matter therefore they must reform, <reference osisRef="Zech.7.9">Zech. vii. 9</reference>. This was what God desired <hi type="italic">more than sacrifices,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Hos. vi. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1 Sam. xv. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen20172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20173" type="x-p"/> III. What little stress God had laid upon the law of sacrifices, though it was his own law, in comparison with the moral precepts (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Did you offer unto me sacrifices in the wilderness forty years?</hi> No, you did not." For the greatest part of that time sacrifice was very much neglected, because of the unsettledness of their state; after the second year, the passover was not kept till they came into Canaan, and other institutions were in like manner intermitted; and yet, because God will have mercy and not sacrifice, he never imputed the omission to them as their fault, but continued his care of them and kindness to them: it was not that, but their murmuring and unbelief, for which God was displeased with them. He that so owned his people, though they did not sacrifice, when in other things they kept close to him, will certainly disown them, though they do sacrifice, if in other things they depart from him. But, though ritual sacrifices may thus be dispensed with, spiritual sacrifices will not; even justice and honesty will not excuse for the want of prayer and praise, a broken heart and the love of God. Stephen quotes this passage (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Acts vii. 42</reference>), to show the Jews that they ought not to think it strange that ceremonial law was repealed when from the beginning it was comparatively made light of. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22-Jer.7.23">Jer. vii. 22, 23</reference>. <div eID="gen20173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20174" type="x-p"/> IV. What little reason they had to expect that their sacrifices should be acceptable to God, when they and their fathers had been all along addicted to the worship of other gods. So some take <reference osisRef="Amos.5.25">v. 25</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Did you offer to me sacrifices,</hi> that is, to me only? No, and therefore not at all to me acceptably;" for the law of worshipping the Lord our God is, <hi type="italic">Him only we must serve.</hi> "<hi type="italic">But you have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">v. 26</reference>), little shrines that you made to carry about with you, pocket-idols for your private superstition, when you durst not be seen to do it publicly. You have had the images of your <hi type="italic">Moloch—your king</hi>" (probably representing <hi type="italic">the sun,</hi> that sits king among the heavenly bodies), "and <hi type="italic">Chiun,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Remphan</hi>" (as Stephen calls it, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">Acts vii. 43</reference>, after the LXX.), which it is supposed, represented Saturn, the highest of the seven planets. The worship of the sun, moon, and stars, was the most ancient, most general, and most plausible idolatry. They <hi type="italic">made to themselves</hi> the <hi type="italic">star of their God,</hi> some particular star which they took to be their god, or the name of which they gave to their god. This idolatry Israel was from the beginning prone to (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>); and those that retain an affection for false gods cannot expect the favour of the true God. <div eID="gen20174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20175" type="x-p"/> V. What punishment God would inflict upon them for their persisting in idolatry (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus.</hi> They were led captive by Satan into idolatry, and therefore God caused them to go into captivity among idolaters, and hurried them into a strange land, since they were so fond of strange gods. They were carried <hi type="italic">beyond Damascus.</hi> Their captivity by the Assyrians was far beyond that by the Syrians; for, if less judgments do not work that for which they were sent, God will send greater. Or the captivity of Israel under Shalmaneser was far beyond that of Damascus under Tiglath-pileser, and much more grievous and destructive, which was foretold <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>. For, as the sins of God's professing people are greater than the sins of others, so it may be expected that their punishments will be proportionable. We find the spoil of Damascus and that of Samaria carried off together by the king of Assyria, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">Isa. viii. 4</reference>. Stephen reads it, <hi type="italic">I will carry you away beyond Babylon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">Acts vii. 43</reference>), further than Judah shall be carried, so far further as not to return. And, to make this sentence appear both the more certain and the more dreadful, he that passes it calls himself <hi type="italic">the Lord, whose name is, The God of hosts,</hi> and who is therefore able to execute the sentence, having hosts at command.  <chapter eID="Amos.5"/> <div eID="gen20175" type="x-p"/>

entries.208e331e6cf06a9c43eaa5e702c32cecffd16c62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12565"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.5.1-Amos.5.27">Am 5:1-27</reference>. Elegy over the Prostrate Kingdom: Renewed Exhortations to Repentance: God Declares that the Coming Day of Judgment Shall Be Terrible to the Scorners Who Despise It: Ceremonial Services Are Not Acceptable to Him Where True Piety Exists Not: Israel Shall Therefore Be Removed Far Eastward.</title> <div sID="gen23148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12565"/><hi type="bold">1. lamentation--</hi>an elegy for the destruction coming on you. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>, "take up," namely, as a mournful burden (<reference osisRef="Ezek.19.1">Eze 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.2">27:2</reference>). <div eID="gen23148" type="x-p"/>
entries.e90d3a047b2707f710c67c008caba4140acb3f8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12566"/><div sID="gen23149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12566"/><hi type="bold">2. virgin of Israel--</hi>the Israelite state heretofore unsubdued by foreigners. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Is 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.13">Jr 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.4">31:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.13">La 2:13</reference>; may be interpreted, Thou who wast once the "virgin daughter of Zion." Rather, "virgin" as applied to a state implies its beauty, and the delights on which it prides itself, its luxuries, power, and wealth [Calvin].<div eID="gen23149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more rise--</hi>in the existing order of things: in the Messianic dispensation it is to rise again, according to many prophecies. Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.23">2Ki 6:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">24:7</reference>, for the restricted sense of "no more."<div eID="gen23150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forsaken upon her land--</hi>or, "prostrated upon," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.5">Eze 29:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.4">32:4</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23151" type="x-p"/>
entries.107cf4803cd7c9eaa38fbb717780381abdeafa7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12567"/><div sID="gen23152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12567"/><hi type="bold">3. went out by a thousand--</hi>that is, "the city from which there used to go out a thousand" equipped for war. "City" is put for "the inhabitants of the city," as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.8">Am 4:8</reference>.<div eID="gen23152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall leave ... hundred--</hi>shall have only a hundred left, the rest being destroyed by sword and pestilence (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.62">De 28:62</reference>). <div eID="gen23153" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5bc51e6db2b205f4f5156d17f36f4576d029254: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12568"/><div sID="gen23154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12568"/><hi type="bold">4. Seek ye me, and ye shall live--</hi>literally, "Seek ... Me, and live." The second imperative expresses the certainty of "life" (escape from judgment) resulting from obedience to the precept in the first imperative. If they perish, it is their own fault; God would forgive, if they would repent (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen23154" type="x-p"/>
entries.60ae00201a2081617b4f785b5cb0a5cdcbaecb1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12569"/><div sID="gen23155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12569"/><hi type="bold">5. seek not Beth-el--</hi>that is, the calves at Beth-el.<div eID="gen23155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilgal--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4">Am 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen23156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beer-sheba--</hi>in Judah on the southern frontier towards Edom. Once "the well of the oath" by Jehovah, ratifying Abraham's covenant with Abimelech, and the scene of his calling on "the Lord, the everlasting God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.31">Ge 21:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.33">33</reference>), now a stronghold of idolatry (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Am 8:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilgal shall surely go into captivity--</hi>a play on similar sounds in the Hebrew, Gilgal, galoh, yigleh: "Gilgal (the place of rolling) shall rolling be rolled away."<div eID="gen23158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beth-el shall come to naught--</hi>Beth-el (that is, the "house of God"), called because of its vain idols Beth-aven (that is, "the house of vanity," or "naught," <reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.5">10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">8</reference>), shall indeed "come to naught." <div eID="gen23159" type="x-p"/>
entries.551b2cc4d6b4a6cf14a364bdc40b7dfa714e5f4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12570"/><div sID="gen23160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12570"/><hi type="bold">6. break out like fire--</hi>bursting through everything in His way. God is "a consuming fire" (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.24">De 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">Is 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">La 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen23160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the house of Joseph--</hi>the kingdom of Israel, of which the tribe of Ephraim, Joseph's son, was the chief tribe (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16">Eze 37:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none to quench it in Beth-el--</hi>that is, none in Beth-el to quench it; none of the Beth-el idols on which Israel so depended, able to remove the divine judgments. <div eID="gen23162" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c3e3dce1d6cea6121190f8227ba71f8e8948647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12571"/><div sID="gen23163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12571"/><hi type="bold">7. turn judgment to wormwood--</hi>that is, pervert it to most bitter wrong. As justice is sweet, so injustice is bitter to the injured. "Wormwood" is from a Hebrew root, to "execrate," on account of its noxious and bitter qualities.<div eID="gen23163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leave on righteousness in ... earth--</hi>Maurer translates, "cast righteousness to the ground," as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Is 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Da 8:12</reference>. <div eID="gen23164" type="x-p"/>
entries.029f009ef5d477445401d0e055a2a2462b52750d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12572"/><div sID="gen23165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12572"/><hi type="bold">8. the seven stars--</hi>literally, the heap or cluster of seven larger stars and others smaller (<reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">38:31</reference>). The former whole passage seems to have been in Amos' mind. He names the stars well known to shepherds (to which class Amos belonged), Orion as the precursor of the tempests which are here threatened, and the Pleiades as ushering in spring.<div eID="gen23165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>Hebraism for the densest darkness.<div eID="gen23166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calleth for the waters of the sea--</hi>both to send deluges in judgment, and the ordinary rain in mercy (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1Ki 18:44</reference>). <div eID="gen23167" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e9b3935488089746dc20e58b88b050ddc084ac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12573"/><div sID="gen23168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12573"/><hi type="bold">9. strengtheneth the spoiled--</hi>literally, "spoil" or "devastation": hence the "person spoiled." Winer, Maurer, and the best modern critics translate, "maketh devastation (or destruction) suddenly to arise," literally, "maketh it to gleam forth like the dawn." Ancient versions support English Version. The Hebrew is elsewhere used, to make, to shine, to make glad: and as English Version here (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>), "recover strength."<div eID="gen23168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spoiled shall come--</hi>"devastation," or "destruction shall come upon" [Maurer]. English Version expresses that, strong as Israel fancies herself after the successes of Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>), even the weakest can be made by God to prevail against the strong. <div eID="gen23169" type="x-p"/>
entries.664448d9c6583a4fcb70e3ab5b2d3b1502995910: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12574"/><div sID="gen23170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12574"/><hi type="bold">10. him that rebuketh in the gate--</hi>the judge who condemns their iniquity in the place of judgment (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Is 29:21</reference>).<div eID="gen23170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abhor him that speaketh uprightly--</hi>the prophet telling them the unwelcome truth: answering in the parallelism to the judge, "that rebuketh in the gate" (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">1Ki 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.8">Pr 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.23">Jr 36:23</reference>). <div eID="gen23171" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ccd56d4158d6b51052e5969d7a99d9d00f6cb95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12575"/><div sID="gen23172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12575"/><hi type="bold">11. burdens of wheat--</hi>burdensome taxes levied in kind from the wheat of the needy, to pamper the lusts of the great [Henderson]. Or wheat advanced in time of scarcity, and exacted again at a burdensome interest [Rabbi Salomon].<div eID="gen23172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">built houses ... but not dwell in them ... vineyards, ... but not drink wine of them--</hi>according to the original prophecy of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">De 28:30</reference>, 38, 39). The converse shall be true in restored Israel (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Am 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.21">Is 65:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen23173" type="x-p"/>
entries.d90f2e6558857d0de0a5de22136a8dff6521568f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12576"/><div sID="gen23174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12576"/><hi type="bold">12. they afflict ... they take--</hi>rather, "(ye) who afflict ... take."<div eID="gen23174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bribe--</hi>literally, a price with which one who has an unjust cause ransoms himself from your sentence (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.35">Pr 6:35</reference>).<div eID="gen23175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn aside the poor in the gate--</hi>refuse them their right in the place of justice (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Am 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Is 29:21</reference>). <div eID="gen23176" type="x-p"/>
entries.c82020a609b8c668a641061cb01ac86fbb6a8fbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12577"/><div sID="gen23177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12577"/><hi type="bold">13. the prudent--</hi>the spiritually wise.<div eID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall keep silence--</hi>not mere silence of tongue, but the prudent shall keep himself quiet from taking part in any public or private affairs which he can avoid: as it is "an evil time," and one in which all law is set at naught. <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">Ep 5:16</reference> refers to this. Instead of impatiently agitating against irremediable evils, the godly wise will not cast pearls before swine, who would trample these, and rend the offerers (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>), but will patiently wait for God's time of deliverance in silent submission (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.9">Psa 39:9</reference>). <div eID="gen23178" type="x-p"/>
entries.860b8796969b5c0bae21229cf8a6b0cace161bae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12578"/><div sID="gen23179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12578"/><hi type="bold">14. and so--</hi>on condition of your "seeking good."<div eID="gen23179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be with you, as ye have spoken--</hi>as ye have boasted; namely, that God is with you, and that you are His people (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen23180" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2a6b0cd5efeecc203ed25dadb09c32c71a88de1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12579"/><div sID="gen23181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12579"/><hi type="bold">15. Hate ... evil ... love ... good--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Is 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.9">Ro 12:9</reference>).<div eID="gen23181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment in the gate--</hi>justice in the place where causes are tried.<div eID="gen23182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it may be that the Lord ... will be gracious--</hi>so, "peradventure" (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.30">Ex 32:30</reference>). Not that men are to come to God with an uncertainty whether or no He will be gracious: the expression merely implies the difficulty in the way, because of the want of true repentance on man's part, so as to stimulate the zealous earnestness of believers in seeking God (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.16.2">Ge 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.14">Joe 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.22">Ac 8:22</reference>).<div eID="gen23183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the remnant of Joseph--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Am 5:6</reference>). Israel (represented by "Ephraim," the leading tribe, and descendant of Joseph) was, as compared to what it once was, now but a remnant, Hazael of Syria having smitten all the coasts from Jordan eastward, Gilead and Bashan, Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2Ki 10:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.33">33</reference>) [Henderson]. Rather, "the remnant of Israel that shall have been left after the wicked have been destroyed" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23184" type="x-p"/>
entries.3460154b72dbbfe4c5dc349254074de006a18112: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12580"/><div sID="gen23185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12580"/><hi type="bold">16. Therefore--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Am 5:13</reference>. God foresees they will not obey the exhortation (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Am 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.15">15</reference>), but will persevere in the unrighteousness stigmatized (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Am 5:7</reference>, 10, 12).<div eID="gen23185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen23186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the God of hosts, the Lord--</hi>an accumulation of titles, of which His lordship over all things is the climax, to mark that from His judgment there is no appeal.<div eID="gen23187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">streets ... highways--</hi>the broad open spaces and the narrow streets common in the East.<div eID="gen23188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call the husbandman to mourning--</hi>The citizens shall call the inexperienced husbandmen to act the part usually performed by professional mourners, as there will not be enough of the latter for the universal mourning which prevails.<div eID="gen23189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">such as are skilful of lamentation--</hi>professional mourners hired to lead off the lamentations for the deceased; alluded to in <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.5">Ec 12:5</reference>; generally women (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.17-Jer.9.19">Jr 9:17-19</reference>). <div eID="gen23190" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1065b219c496c17d1f78beee16d05a9300bbc45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12581"/><div sID="gen23191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12581"/><hi type="bold">17. in all vineyards ... wailing--</hi>where usually songs of joy were heard.<div eID="gen23191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pass through thee--</hi>taking vengeance (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Ex 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>). "Pass over" and "pass by," on the contrary, are used of God's forgiving (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">Ex 12:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">Am 7:8</reference>). <div eID="gen23192" type="x-p"/>
entries.4908f5b2e05e3d6ec13e7510401107bc1a0dc50f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12582"/><div sID="gen23193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12582"/>18. Woe unto you who do not scruple to say in irony, "We desire that the day of the Lord would come," that is, "Woe to you who treat it as if it were a mere dream of the prophets" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Is 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.15">Jr 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>).<div eID="gen23193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to what end is it for you!--</hi>Amos taking their ironical words in earnest: for God often takes the blasphemer at his own word, in righteous retribution making the scoffer's jest a terrible reality against himself. Ye have but little reason to desire the day of the Lord; for it will be to you calamity, and not joy. <div eID="gen23194" type="x-p"/>
entries.2afd8b1a462f0eb3b98515848e59e1588d47c30a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12583"/><div sID="gen23195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12583"/><hi type="bold">19. As if a man did flee ... a lion, and a bear met him--</hi>Trying to escape one calamity, he falls into another. This perhaps implies that in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference> their ironical desire for the day of the Lord was as if it would be an escape from existing calamities. The coming of the day of the Lord would be good news to us, if true: for we have served God (that is, the golden calves). So do hypocrites flatter themselves as to death and judgment, as if these would be a relief from existing ills of life. The lion may from generosity spare the prostrate, but the bear spares none (compare <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Is 24:18</reference>).<div eID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaned ... on the wall--</hi>on the side wall of the house, to support himself from falling. Snakes often hid themselves in fissures in a wall. Those not reformed by God's judgments will be pursued by them: if they escape one, another is ready to seize them. <div eID="gen23196" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dc0e28b10236335ba1dd5d324999b060a8c2cdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12584"/><div sID="gen23197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12584"/><hi type="bold">21. I hate, I despise--</hi>The two verbs joined without a conjunction express God's strong abhorrence.<div eID="gen23197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your feast days--</hi>yours; not Mine; I do not acknowledge them: unlike those in Judah, yours are of human, not divine institution.<div eID="gen23198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will not smell--</hi>that is, I will take no delight in the sacrifices offered (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Ge 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">Le 26:31</reference>).<div eID="gen23199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in your solemn assemblies--</hi>literally, "days of restraint." <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10-Isa.1.15">Is 1:10-15</reference> is parallel. Isaiah is fuller; Amos, more condensed. Amos condemns Israel not only on the ground of their thinking to satisfy God by sacrifices without obedience (the charge brought by Isaiah against the Jews), but also because even their external ritual was a mere corruption, and unsanctioned by God. <div eID="gen23200" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1b5b8eebf541c3fbada7cd528c32a4caa17f124: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12585"/><div sID="gen23201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12585"/><hi type="bold">22. meat offerings--</hi>flour, &c. Unbloody offerings.<div eID="gen23201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace offerings--</hi>offerings for obtaining from God peace and prosperity. Hebrew, "thank offerings." <div eID="gen23202" type="x-p"/>
entries.3667ecf26860370eeed5a83cd4877de8aae04252: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12586"/><div sID="gen23203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12586"/><hi type="bold">23. Take ... away from me--</hi>literally, "Take away, from upon Me"; the idea being that of a burden pressing upon the bearer. So <reference osisRef="Isa.1.14">Is 1:14</reference>, "They are a trouble unto Me (literally, 'a burden upon Me'): I am weary to bear them."<div eID="gen23203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the noise of thy songs--</hi>The hymns and instrumental music on sacred occasions are to Me nothing but a disagreeable noise.<div eID="gen23204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will not hear--</hi>Isaiah substitutes "prayers" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>) for the "songs" and "melody" here; but, like Amos, closes with "I will not hear." <div eID="gen23205" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6617320f0ea7b8168cf82b8bb39b26d14e38114: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12587"/><div sID="gen23206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12587"/><hi type="bold">24. judgment--</hi>justice.<div eID="gen23206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run down--</hi>literally, "roll," that is, flow abundantly (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">Is 48:18</reference>). Without the desire to fulfil righteousness in the offerer, the sacrifice is hateful to God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mi 6:8</reference>). <div eID="gen23207" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1ebe46d69715f46c413b0ac8ed10b5128806a2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12588"/><div sID="gen23208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12588"/><hi type="bold">25-26. Have ye offered? &c.--</hi>Yes: ye have. "But (all the time with strange inconsistency) ye have borne (aloft in solemn pomp) the tabernacle (that is, the portable shrine, or model tabernacle: small enough not to be detected by Moses; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.19.24">Ac 19:24</reference>) of your Molech" (that idol is "your" god; I am not, though ye go through the form of presenting offerings to Me). The question, "Have ye," is not a denial (for they did offer in the wilderness to Jehovah sacrifices of the cattle which they took with them in their nomad life there, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.4">Ex 24:4</reference>; Nu 7:1-89; 9:1, &c.), but a strong affirmation (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27">1Sa 2:27</reference>, 28; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">Eze 20:4</reference>). The sin of Israel in Amos' time is the very sin of their forefathers, mocking God with worship, while at the same time worshipping idols (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference>). It was clandestine in Moses' time, else he would have put it down; he was aware generally of their unfaithfulness, though not knowing the particulars (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">De 31:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen23208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Molech ... Chiun--</hi>"Molech" means "king" answering to Mars [Bengel]; the Sun [Jablonski]; Saturn, the same as "Chiun" [Maurer]. The Septuagint translates "Chiun" into Remphan, as Stephen quotes it (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Ac 7:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">43</reference>). The same god often had different names. Molech is the Ammonite name; Chiun, the Arabic and Persian name, written also Chevan. In an Arabic lexicon Chiun means "austere"; so astrologers represented Saturn as a planet baleful in his influence. Hence the Phoenicians offered human sacrifices to him, children especially; so idolatrous Israel also. Rimmon was the Syrian name (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.18">2Ki 5:18</reference>); pronounced as Remvan, or "Remphan," just as Chiun was also Chevan. Molech had the form of a king; Chevan, or Chiun, of a star [Grotius]. Remphan was the Egyptian name for Saturn: hence the Septuagint translator of Amos gave the Egyptian name for the Hebrew, being an Egyptian. [Hodius II, De Bibliorum Textibus Originalibus. 4.115]. The same as the Nile, of which the Egyptians made the star Saturn the representative [Harenberg]. Bengel considers Remphan or Rephan akin to Teraphim and Remphis, the name of a king of Egypt.
